items.title: Physics & Astrophysics Greats — Raman, Bose, Saha, Chandrasekhar
items.body:
### The physicists who put India on the map

**In one line**
A handful of Indian physicists made discoveries about light, particles and stars that are still named after them and still appear in exams.

**The story**
In 1928 **C.V. Raman** noticed that when light passes through a liquid, a tiny part of it changes colour — the **Raman Effect**. This won him the **1930 Nobel Prize in Physics**, the first science Nobel for any Asian, and 28 February (the day of his discovery) is now **National Science Day**. Around the same time **S.N. Bose** worked out the statistics of light particles; Einstein extended it, giving **Bose–Einstein statistics**, and the whole family of such particles — **bosons** — is named after Bose. **Meghnad Saha** gave an equation (1920) explaining how hot gases in stars become ionised, the foundation of reading stellar spectra. A generation later **S. Chandrasekhar** — Raman's nephew — calculated the **Chandrasekhar limit (~1.44 solar masses)**, the heaviest a white-dwarf star can be before it collapses, work that earned the **1983 Nobel Physics**. Separately, **J.C. Bose** demonstrated wireless communication using radio (microwave) waves in Kolkata in 1895, before Marconi's public demonstration; he invented the **crescograph** to measure plant growth and response to stimuli, and founded the **Bose Institute, Kolkata (1917)**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
APPSC asks 'who discovered/is named after what', Nobel years, National Science Day, and the Raman–Chandrasekhar family link; match-the-following is common.

**Picture it**

| Scientist | Signature contribution | Top honour |
|---|---|---|
| C.V. Raman | Raman Effect (light scattering) | Nobel Physics 1930; Bharat Ratna 1954 |
| S.N. Bose | Bose–Einstein statistics | the 'boson' named after him |
| Meghnad Saha | thermal ionization equation | FRS |
| S. Chandrasekhar | Chandrasekhar limit (~1.44 M☉) | Nobel Physics 1983 |
| J.C. Bose | crescograph; pre-Marconi wireless | Bose Institute (1917) |

**Terms explained**
- **Raman Effect** — the slight change in a light ray's colour when it scatters off molecules.
- **Boson** — a class of particle (like the photon) that obeys Bose–Einstein statistics.
- **Chandrasekhar limit** — the maximum mass (~1.44 times the Sun) of a stable white-dwarf star.
- **Crescograph** — J.C. Bose's instrument to measure very small plant movements/growth.

**Don't confuse**
- **S.N. Bose vs J.C. Bose** — S.N. Bose = bosons/quantum statistics; J.C. Bose = plant science and wireless.
- **Raman vs Chandrasekhar** — Raman = light scattering (1930 Nobel); Chandrasekhar = white-dwarf limit (1983 Nobel); they were uncle and nephew.

**Remember it**
Physics four = Raman, Bose, Saha, Chandrasekhar — "**R**eally **B**right **S**tars **C**luster".

**TL;DR**
- C.V. Raman: Raman Effect (1928), Nobel Physics 1930, Bharat Ratna 1954; 28 Feb = National Science Day.
- S.N. Bose gave Bose–Einstein statistics; the 'boson' is named after him.
- Meghnad Saha gave the thermal ionization equation, foundational to astrophysics.
- S. Chandrasekhar (Raman's nephew): Chandrasekhar limit ~1.44 M☉; Nobel Physics 1983.
- J.C. Bose: pre-Marconi wireless, the crescograph, and the Bose Institute (1917).
keyPoints: C.V. Raman discovered the Raman Effect (28 Feb 1928), won Nobel Physics 1930, and got the Bharat Ratna in 1954; 28 Feb is National Science Day.
S.N. Bose gave Bose–Einstein statistics; the 'boson' is named after him.
Meghnad Saha formulated the Saha thermal ionization equation, foundational to astrophysics.
S. Chandrasekhar gave the Chandrasekhar limit (~1.44 solar masses) and won the Nobel Physics prize in 1983.
Chandrasekhar was C.V. Raman's nephew.
J.C. Bose demonstrated wireless/microwave communication before Marconi, invented the crescograph, and founded the Bose Institute (1917).
items.mnemonic: Physics four = Raman, Bose, Saha, Chandrasekhar — 'Really Bright Stars Cluster'.

items.title: Institution Builders — Bhabha, Sarabhai, Bhatnagar, P.C. Ray
items.body:
### Scientists who built India's research base

**In one line**
Some Indian scientists are remembered less for a single discovery than for the lasting institutions — TIFR, ISRO, the CSIR labs — they created.

**The story**
After independence, a few scientists turned personal brilliance into permanent national capability. **Homi J. Bhabha**, the **father of India's nuclear programme**, gave the **cascade theory** of cosmic-ray showers but is remembered for founding **TIFR (1945)**, heading the **Atomic Energy Commission**, and designing the **three-stage nuclear power programme**; BARC at Trombay is named after him. **Vikram Sarabhai**, the **father of the Indian space programme**, founded the **Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad (1947)** and **INCOSPAR**, which became **ISRO (1969)**. **S.S. Bhatnagar**, first Director-General of **CSIR**, built India's chain of national laboratories; the top science prize for researchers under 45 is named after him. **P.C. Ray**, the **father of the Indian pharmaceutical industry**, founded Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works. **C.N.R. Rao**, a materials chemist, founded **JNCASR, Bengaluru**, and received the **Bharat Ratna in 2014** (the third scientist to be honoured, after Raman and Kalam).

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
These founders explain the institutions behind Paper-II and Mains policy questions; 'who founded what' and 'father of which programme' are repeat items.

**Picture it**

| Scientist | Built / is 'father of' |
|---|---|
| Homi Bhabha | nuclear programme; TIFR, AEC, BARC |
| Vikram Sarabhai | space programme; PRL, INCOSPAR → ISRO |
| S.S. Bhatnagar | first DG of CSIR; national labs; SSB Prize |
| P.C. Ray | Indian pharma industry; Bengal Chemical |
| C.N.R. Rao | JNCASR; Bharat Ratna 2014 |

**Terms explained**
- **TIFR** — Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, founded by Bhabha in 1945.
- **INCOSPAR** — the committee Sarabhai set up that became ISRO.
- **CSIR** — Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, the national lab network Bhatnagar led.
- **SSB Prize** — the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize, India's top award for scientists under 45.

**Don't confuse**
- **Bhabha vs Sarabhai** — Bhabha = nuclear (TIFR/BARC); Sarabhai = space (PRL/ISRO).
- **Bhatnagar vs the Raman Effect** — Bhatnagar built CSIR; the Raman Effect is Raman's, not his.

**Remember it**
Builders 'B-S-B-R' = **B**habha (atom), **S**arabhai (space), **B**hatnagar (CSIR), **R**ay (pharma).

**TL;DR**
- Bhabha: father of the nuclear programme; founded TIFR; three-stage programme; BARC named after him.
- Sarabhai: father of the space programme; founded PRL and INCOSPAR (seed of ISRO, 1969).
- Bhatnagar: first DG of CSIR; the SSB Prize is named after him.
- P.C. Ray: father of the Indian pharmaceutical industry; C.N.R. Rao founded JNCASR, Bharat Ratna 2014.
keyPoints: Homi Bhabha: father of India's nuclear programme; founded TIFR; conceived the three-stage nuclear programme; BARC named after him.
Vikram Sarabhai: father of the Indian space programme; founded PRL Ahmedabad and INCOSPAR (forerunner of ISRO).
S.S. Bhatnagar: first DG of CSIR; the SSB Prize for scientists under 45 is named after him.
P.C. Ray: father of the Indian pharmaceutical industry; founded Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works.
C.N.R. Rao: solid-state/materials chemist, founded JNCASR, and received the Bharat Ratna in 2014.

items.title: Indian-origin Nobel & Global Laureates — Khorana, Ramakrishnan, Ramanujan
items.body:
### Global recognition for Indian-origin scientists

**In one line**
Several scientists of Indian origin won the world's highest honours abroad — two science Nobels and a mathematics legend elected to the Royal Society.

**The story**
**Har Gobind Khorana** shared the **1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine** for working out how the **genetic code** directs the building of proteins; he later made the first chemical synthesis of a gene. Four decades on, **Venkatraman Ramakrishnan** shared the **2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for mapping the atomic structure of the **ribosome**, the cell's protein factory, and went on to become President of the Royal Society, London. Earlier still, the self-taught genius **Srinivasa Ramanujan** produced astonishing results in **pure mathematics** — **number theory, infinite series and continued fractions** — collaborating with **G.H. Hardy** at Cambridge and being elected **FRS in 1918**. His birthday, **22 December**, is India's **National Mathematics Day**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
Matching a laureate to the Nobel year and field, and 'whose birthday is National Mathematics Day', are standard recall items; consolidated 'who all won a science Nobel' statements appear too.

**Picture it**

| Laureate | Year | Field | For |
|---|---|---|---|
| C.V. Raman | 1930 | Physics | Raman Effect |
| Har Gobind Khorana | 1968 | Medicine | genetic code |
| S. Chandrasekhar | 1983 | Physics | white-dwarf limit |
| Venkatraman Ramakrishnan | 2009 | Chemistry | ribosome structure |

**Terms explained**
- **Genetic code** — the rules by which DNA sequences specify proteins.
- **Ribosome** — the cell structure that assembles proteins; Ramakrishnan mapped its atoms.
- **FRS** — Fellow of the Royal Society, a top scientific honour in the UK.

**Don't confuse**
- **Khorana (1968, Medicine) vs Ramakrishnan (2009, Chemistry)** — different years and fields.
- **Ramanujan has no Nobel** — there is no Nobel for mathematics; his honour was FRS and National Mathematics Day.

**Remember it**
Science Nobels timeline: "Raman 1930 → Khorana 1968 → Chandrasekhar 1983 → Ramakrishnan 2009".

**TL;DR**
- Har Gobind Khorana shared the 1968 Nobel (Medicine) for interpreting the genetic code.
- Venkatraman Ramakrishnan shared the 2009 Nobel (Chemistry) for the ribosome structure.
- Ramanujan (number theory, infinite series) worked with G.H. Hardy, was FRS 1918; 22 Dec = National Mathematics Day.
- Science Nobel laureates linked to India: Raman (1930), Khorana (1968), Chandrasekhar (1983), Ramakrishnan (2009).
keyPoints: Har Gobind Khorana shared the 1968 Nobel (Medicine) for interpreting the genetic code.
Venkatraman Ramakrishnan shared the 2009 Nobel (Chemistry) for the ribosome structure.
Ramanujan's birthday (22 December) is National Mathematics Day; he worked with G.H. Hardy and was FRS in 1918.
Science Nobel laureates linked to India: Raman (1930), Khorana (1968), Chandrasekhar (1983), Ramakrishnan (2009).
items.mnemonic: Science Nobels timeline: Raman 1930 → Khorana 1968 → Chandrasekhar 1983 → Ramakrishnan 2009.

items.title: Applied Science for the Nation — Kalam, Swaminathan, Kurien
items.body:
### Science that transformed everyday India

**In one line**
Three scientists turned research into national self-reliance — Kalam in defence and space, Swaminathan in food, Kurien in milk.

**The story**
**A.P.J. Abdul Kalam**, the 'Missile Man', was project director of **SLV-III (1980)**, India's first satellite launch vehicle, led the **Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP)** (Agni, Prithvi), was central to the **Pokhran-II nuclear tests (1998)**, and served as **President of India (2002–07)**; he received the **Bharat Ratna in 1997**. **M.S. Swaminathan**, the **father of the Green Revolution**, worked with Norman Borlaug to introduce **high-yielding wheat and rice**, turning India from food-importer to food-surplus; he was awarded the **Bharat Ratna in 2024 (posthumous)**. **Verghese Kurien**, the **father of the White Revolution**, built the **Amul** cooperative model and led **Operation Flood** through the **NDDB**, making India the world's largest milk producer.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
These three are the ready-made 'science for national development / Atmanirbhar Bharat' examples for Mains Paper-5, and 'who led which revolution' is a frequent Prelims item.

**Picture it**

| Scientist | Field | Signature work | Honour |
|---|---|---|---|
| A.P.J. Abdul Kalam | defence/space | SLV-III, IGMDP, Pokhran-II | Bharat Ratna 1997; President 2002–07 |
| M.S. Swaminathan | agriculture | Green Revolution (HYV wheat/rice) | Bharat Ratna 2024 (posthumous) |
| Verghese Kurien | dairy | Operation Flood, Amul, NDDB | world's largest milk producer |

**Terms explained**
- **SLV-III** — Satellite Launch Vehicle-3, India's first, which put Rohini into orbit in 1980.
- **Green Revolution** — the big rise in food-grain output from high-yielding seeds, irrigation and fertiliser.
- **White Revolution / Operation Flood** — the dairy-cooperative programme that made India the top milk producer.

**Don't confuse**
- **Green vs White Revolution** — Green = food grains (Swaminathan); White = milk (Kurien).
- **Kalam's two hats** — a space/missile scientist who also became President; the SDSC spaceport is named after Satish Dhawan, not Kalam.

**Remember it**
Three revolutions of self-reliance: **Kalam** (defence/space), **Swaminathan** (Green/food), **Kurien** (White/milk).

**TL;DR**
- Kalam directed SLV-III and the IGMDP missiles, was central to Pokhran-II (1998), President 2002–07, Bharat Ratna 1997.
- Swaminathan is the father of India's Green Revolution; Bharat Ratna 2024 (posthumous).
- Kurien is the father of the White Revolution; led Operation Flood, Amul and the NDDB.
- Together they anchor a 'science for national self-reliance' argument in Mains Paper-5.
keyPoints: A.P.J. Abdul Kalam directed SLV-III and the IGMDP missiles, was central to Pokhran-II (1998), President 2002–07, Bharat Ratna 1997.
M.S. Swaminathan is the father of India's Green Revolution; Bharat Ratna 2024 (posthumous).
Verghese Kurien is the father of the White Revolution; led Operation Flood, Amul and the NDDB.
Together they anchor a 'science for national self-reliance' argument in Mains Paper-V.
items.mnemonic: Three revolutions of self-reliance: Kalam (defence/space), Swaminathan (Green/food), Kurien (White/milk).

items.title: Andhra Connection & Contemporary Women Scientists
items.body:
### Andhra Pradesh's own and today's women scientists

**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh gave the world the biochemist Yellapragada Subbarao, while a new generation of women are leading India's missile and space missions.

**The story**
**Yellapragada Subbarao**, born on **12 January 1895 at Bhimavaram (West Godavari, AP)**, was a biochemist who synthesised **folic acid**, developed the anti-cancer drug **methotrexate**, discovered **diethylcarbamazine (DEC)** for filariasis, and helped reveal the role of **ATP** in muscular energy — yet remained largely unrecognised in his lifetime while working at Lederle Laboratories, USA. Andhra also has a link to **C.V. Raman**, who studied at **Mrs A.V.N. College, Visakhapatnam**. Today, women scientists lead flagship missions: **Tessy Thomas**, DRDO's 'Missile Woman', was Project Director of the **Agni-IV/V** missiles; **Ritu Karidhal**, ISRO's 'Rocket Woman', held mission-director roles in **Mangalyaan** and **Chandrayaan**; and **Nigar Shaji** was Project Director of the **Aditya-L1** solar mission (launched September 2023).

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
The AP-born Subbarao and his discoveries are a strong state-specific item; current women scientists and their missions are topical match-the-following questions.

**Picture it**

| Scientist | Organisation | Known for |
|---|---|---|
| Y. Subbarao | Lederle (USA) | folic acid, methotrexate, DEC, ATP role |
| Tessy Thomas | DRDO | Agni missiles |
| Ritu Karidhal | ISRO | Mars (Mangalyaan) / Moon (Chandrayaan) |
| Nigar Shaji | ISRO | Aditya-L1 solar mission |

**Terms explained**
- **Folic acid** — a B-vitamin Subbarao first synthesised; vital in treating anaemia.
- **Methotrexate** — a drug (from Subbarao's work) used against cancer and arthritis.
- **Aditya-L1** — ISRO's first solar observation mission, launched in 2023.

**Don't confuse**
- **Tessy Thomas vs Ritu Karidhal** — Thomas (DRDO) = Agni missiles; Karidhal (ISRO) = Mars/Moon missions.
- **Subbarao's discoveries** — folic acid and methotrexate (not the Raman Effect or the Chandrasekhar limit).

**Remember it**
AP biochemist Subbarao = "**Folic–Metho–DEC–ATP**" — four life-saving contributions.

**TL;DR**
- Yellapragada Subbarao (born Bhimavaram, AP) synthesised folic acid and methotrexate and discovered diethylcarbamazine.
- C.V. Raman studied at Mrs A.V.N. College, Visakhapatnam.
- Tessy Thomas ('Missile Woman', DRDO) was Project Director of the Agni missiles.
- Ritu Karidhal (ISRO) led Mangalyaan/Chandrayaan roles; Nigar Shaji was PD of Aditya-L1 (2023).
keyPoints: Yellapragada Subbarao (born Bhimavaram, AP) synthesised folic acid and methotrexate and discovered diethylcarbamazine for filariasis.
C.V. Raman studied at Mrs A.V.N. College, Visakhapatnam.
Tessy Thomas ('Missile Woman') was Project Director of the Agni missiles at DRDO.
Ritu Karidhal ('Rocket Woman') held mission-director roles in Mangalyaan and Chandrayaan.
Nigar Shaji was Project Director of ISRO's Aditya-L1 solar mission (2023).
items.mnemonic: AP biochemist Subbarao = 'Folic-Metho-DEC-ATP' — four life-saving discoveries.

items.title: Ancient & Medieval Indian Scientists — Mathematics, Astronomy & Medicine
items.body:
## Science in ancient India

**In one line:** Indian mathematicians gave the world zero and the decimal place-value system, astronomers explained the Earth's rotation, and physicians wrote the first great texts of surgery and medicine.

**Why it is asked:** "author of Aryabhatiya", "father of surgery", "Lilavati was written by" and "rules for zero" are classic PSC culture-science questions.

**The story**

**Aryabhata** (born 476 CE) wrote the **Aryabhatiya** (499 CE), used the place-value system, gave a close value of pi and said the Earth rotates on its axis — India's first satellite (1975) was named after him. **Brahmagupta** (7th century) wrote the **Brahmasphutasiddhanta** with the first rules for arithmetic with **zero**. **Bhaskara II** (12th century) wrote **Lilavati** and the **Siddhanta Shiromani**. In medicine, the **Charaka Samhita** is the classic of internal medicine (Ayurveda), and **Sushruta**, called the **father of surgery**, described plastic surgery (rhinoplasty) in the **Sushruta Samhita**.

### Ancient and medieval scientists

| Scientist | Work / contribution |
|---|---|
| **Aryabhata (born 476 CE)** | Aryabhatiya (499 CE) — place value, value of pi, Earth rotates on its axis |
| **Brahmagupta (7th century)** | Brahmasphutasiddhanta — first rules for arithmetic with zero |
| **Bhaskara II (12th century)** | Lilavati and Siddhanta Shiromani |
| **Varahamihira (6th century)** | Pancha Siddhantika and Brihat Samhita (astronomy and astrology) |
| **Sushruta** | Sushruta Samhita — "father of surgery"; plastic surgery (rhinoplasty) |
| **Charaka** | Charaka Samhita — classic of Ayurvedic internal medicine |
| **Baudhayana** | Sulba Sutra — stated the "Pythagoras" theorem long before Pythagoras |
| **Kanada** | Vaisheshika school — early atomic theory (anu, parmanu) |
| **Madhava of Sangamagrama (14th century)** | Kerala school — infinite series for pi and trigonometric functions |
| **Nagarjuna (alchemist)** | Rasaratnakara — rasayana (alchemy and metallurgy of mercury) |
| **Lagadha** | Vedanga Jyotisha — earliest Indian astronomical text |

## Don't confuse
- **Aryabhata = Aryabhatiya (499 CE); Brahmagupta = rules for zero; Bhaskara II = Lilavati.**
- **Sushruta = surgery; Charaka = medicine.**
- **Nagarjuna the alchemist** is a different person from the Buddhist philosopher Nagarjuna of Nagarjunakonda.

**Remember it:** "A-B-B: Aryabhata (5th c.) → Brahmagupta (7th c.) → Bhaskara II (12th c.)."

**TL;DR**
- Aryabhatiya 499 CE: place value, pi, rotation of the Earth; India's first satellite was named Aryabhata.
- Brahmagupta gave the rules for zero; Bhaskara II wrote Lilavati.
- Sushruta = father of surgery (rhinoplasty); Charaka = Ayurvedic medicine.
keyPoints: Aryabhata (born 476 CE) — Aryabhatiya (499 CE) — place value, value of pi, Earth rotates on its axis.
Brahmagupta (7th century) — Brahmasphutasiddhanta — first rules for arithmetic with zero.

items.title: More Modern Indian Scientists — Who Did What
items.body:
## A wider gallery of modern Indian science

**In one line:** beyond the Nobel and institution-builder names, PSC papers ask about statisticians, ornithologists, botanists, nuclear and space leaders, women pioneers and astronauts.

**Why it is asked:** "Birdman of India", "Mahalanobis founded?", "Pokhran-I was led by?", "first Indian in space" and "current ISRO chairman" are frequent match and direct items.

**The story**

**P.C. Mahalanobis** founded the **Indian Statistical Institute (1931)** and drafted the Second Five-Year Plan model. **Salim Ali** became the "Birdman of India". **Raja Ramanna** led **Pokhran-I (1974)**. **Satish Dhawan** steered ISRO from 1972 to 1984, and the Sriharikota launch centre bears his name. **Rakesh Sharma** became the first Indian in space in **1984** aboard **Soyuz T-11**. In **2025**, **Shubhanshu Shukla** flew on **Axiom-4** and became the **first Indian to visit the International Space Station**. **V. Narayanan** has headed ISRO since **January 2025**, after **S. Somanath** (2022–2025), who led Chandrayaan-3.

### Scientists and their contributions

| Scientist | Known for |
|---|---|
| **P.C. Mahalanobis** | founded the Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata (1931); Mahalanobis distance; Second Five-Year Plan model |
| **Salim Ali** | "Birdman of India" — ornithologist |
| **Birbal Sahni** | palaeobotany — Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences, Lucknow |
| **G.N. Ramachandran** | Ramachandran plot — structure of proteins; triple helix of collagen |
| **Satish Dhawan** | ISRO chairman 1972–84; father of experimental fluid dynamics in India; SDSC-SHAR named after him |
| **U.R. Rao** | led India's first satellite Aryabhata (1975); ISRO chairman 1984–94 |
| **K. Kasturirangan** | ISRO chairman 1994–2003; chaired the drafting committee of the National Education Policy 2020 (died 2025) |
| **Raja Ramanna** | led India's first nuclear test, Pokhran-I (1974) |
| **R. Chidambaram** | key role in Pokhran-I and Pokhran-II; Principal Scientific Adviser 2001–2018 |
| **Jayant Narlikar** | Hoyle–Narlikar theory of gravity; founded IUCAA, Pune (died 2025) |
| **M. Visvesvaraya** | engineer (Krishna Raja Sagara dam); Bharat Ratna 1955; his birthday, 15 September, is Engineers' Day |
| **S. Somanath** | ISRO chairman 2022–2025 — Chandrayaan-3 Moon landing and Aditya-L1 |
| **V. Narayanan** | ISRO chairman from January 2025 (cryogenic propulsion expert) |
| **K. Sivan** | ISRO chairman 2018–2022 — Chandrayaan-2 |
| **Sam Pitroda** | telecom revolution — founded C-DOT (1984) |
| **Ronald Ross** | showed mosquitoes carry malaria (1897, at Secunderabad); Nobel Prize in Medicine 1902 |

### Women scientists and Indians in space

| Person | Known for |
|---|---|
| **E.K. Janaki Ammal** | botanist — sweet sugarcane hybrids; first Indian woman PhD in botany (1931) |
| **Anna Mani** | "Weather Woman of India" — meteorological instruments at IMD |
| **Asima Chatterjee** | chemist — anti-epileptic and anti-malarial drugs from plants (vinca alkaloids) |
| **Kamala Sohonie** | first Indian woman to earn a PhD in a science discipline (biochemistry) |
| **Rakesh Sharma** | first Indian in space — Soyuz T-11, April 1984 |
| **Kalpana Chawla** | first woman of Indian origin in space (1997); died in the Columbia disaster (2003) |
| **Shubhanshu Shukla** | Axiom-4 (June–July 2025) — first Indian aboard the International Space Station; Gaganyaan astronaut-designate |
| **Sunita Williams** | Indian-origin NASA astronaut; Boeing Starliner test flight (2024), returned in March 2025 |

## Don't confuse
- **Rakesh Sharma (1984, Soyuz T-11)** was the first Indian in space; **Shubhanshu Shukla (2025, Axiom-4)** was the first Indian on the **ISS**. **Kalpana Chawla** was the first **Indian-origin woman** in space.
- **Raja Ramanna = Pokhran-I (1974); Kalam and Chidambaram = Pokhran-II (1998).**
- **ISRO chairmen in order:** Sarabhai, then Dhawan (1972–84), then U.R. Rao, Kasturirangan, Sivan (2018–22), Somanath (2022–25) and V. Narayanan (2025–).

**Remember it:** "Salim = birds, Sahni = fossils, Mahalanobis = statistics, Janaki Ammal = sugarcane."

**TL;DR**
- Mahalanobis founded the ISI (1931); Salim Ali is the Birdman of India; Visvesvaraya's birthday is Engineers' Day (15 September).
- Kasturirangan chaired the NEP 2020 drafting committee; Narlikar founded IUCAA (both died in 2025).
- ISRO chairman since January 2025: V. Narayanan. Shukla went to the ISS on Axiom-4 (2025).
keyPoints: P.C. Mahalanobis — founded the Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata (1931); Mahalanobis distance; Second Five-Year Plan model.
Salim Ali — "Birdman of India" — ornithologist.
E.K. Janaki Ammal — botanist — sweet sugarcane hybrids; first Indian woman PhD in botany (1931).
Rakesh Sharma — first Indian in space — Soyuz T-11, April 1984.

items.title: Honours for Scientists & More Scientists from Andhra Pradesh
items.body:
## Who got which honour, and the Telugu scientists APPSC asks about

**In one line:** only five scientists or engineers have received the Bharat Ratna, a few Indian-origin mathematicians have won the Fields or Abel prizes, and several Telugu scientists built national institutions.

**Why it is asked:** "which scientist was not awarded the Bharat Ratna?", "first Vigyan Ratna", and AP-angle questions on C.R. Rao, Y. Nayudamma, K.L. Rao and S. Bhagavantam recur in APPSC papers.

**The story**

The Bharat Ratna has gone to **C.V. Raman (1954)**, **M. Visvesvaraya (1955)**, **A.P.J. Abdul Kalam (1997)**, **C.N.R. Rao (2014)** and **M.S. Swaminathan (2024, posthumous)**; Homi Bhabha and Vikram Sarabhai never received it. In 2023 the government replaced the many ministry science prizes with the **Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar**, and the first **Vigyan Ratna (2024)** went to biochemist **G. Padmanabhan**. Among Telugu scientists, statistician **C.R. Rao** won the **International Prize in Statistics (2023)**, leather technologist **Y. Nayudamma** directed the **CLRI**, engineer **K.L. Rao** proposed the **Ganga–Cauvery link**, and physicist **S. Bhagavantam**, Raman's colleague, became scientific adviser to the Defence Minister.

### Honours won by scientists

| Honour | Scientist(s) |
|---|---|
| **Bharat Ratna 1954** | C.V. Raman |
| **Bharat Ratna 1955** | M. Visvesvaraya |
| **Bharat Ratna 1997** | A.P.J. Abdul Kalam |
| **Bharat Ratna 2014** | C.N.R. Rao |
| **Bharat Ratna 2024 (posthumous)** | M.S. Swaminathan |
| **First Vigyan Ratna (Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar, 2024)** | G. Padmanabhan (biochemist) |
| **Fields Medal 2014 (Indian-origin)** | Manjul Bhargava |
| **Abel Prize 2007 (Indian-born)** | S.R. Srinivasa Varadhan |
| **Fields Medal 2018 (Indian-origin)** | Akshay Venkatesh |

### More scientists linked to Andhra Pradesh

| Scientist | Known for |
|---|---|
| **C.R. Rao (Calyampudi Radhakrishna Rao)** | statistician — Cramér–Rao bound, Rao–Blackwell theorem; International Prize in Statistics 2023 (died 2023) |
| **Yelavarthy Nayudamma (Guntur district)** | leather technologist; Director of CLRI Chennai; Director-General of CSIR (died in the 1985 Kanishka crash) |
| **K.L. Rao (Krishna district)** | irrigation engineer — designed Nagarjuna Sagar; proposed the Ganga–Cauvery link; Union Irrigation Minister |
| **S. Bhagavantam** | physicist and Raman's colleague; Andhra University; scientific adviser to the Defence Minister |
| **K. Rangadhama Rao** | spectroscopist at Andhra University, Waltair |
| **M. Visvesvaraya** | family roots in Mokshagundam village (Prakasam district, AP) |

## Don't confuse
- **Bharat Ratna scientists:** Raman 1954, Visvesvaraya 1955, Kalam 1997, C.N.R. Rao 2014, Swaminathan 2024. **Bhabha and Sarabhai never got it** (both received the Padma Bhushan).
- **C.R. Rao** (statistics, Telugu) is a different person from **C.N.R. Rao** (chemistry, Bharat Ratna 2014).
- **Nayudamma = leather (CLRI); K.L. Rao = dams and river links; Y. Subbarao = drugs (folic acid).**

**Remember it:** "Ra-Vi-Ka-Ra-Swa: Raman, Visvesvaraya, Kalam, Rao, Swaminathan."

**TL;DR**
- Five science or engineering Bharat Ratnas, from 1954 to 2024.
- First Vigyan Ratna (2024): G. Padmanabhan. Fields Medal: Manjul Bhargava (2014). Abel Prize: S.R.S. Varadhan (2007).
- AP links: C.R. Rao, Y. Nayudamma, K.L. Rao, S. Bhagavantam and Y. Subbarao.

Yelavarthy Nayudamma (Guntur district) — leather technologist; Director of CLRI Chennai; Director-General of CSIR (died in the 1985 Kanishka crash).

items.title: For Mains — Indian scientists & nation-building
items.body:
**In one line**
For Mains (Paper-5, clause M5-1 'institutes in AP & India; scientists'), individual scientists are used as evidence in a larger argument about how science, institutions and policy together built modern India.

**The analytical frame**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Discovery → capability | individual genius (Raman, Bose, Chandrasekhar) becomes national strength only when institutionalised |
| Institution-building | Bhabha (TIFR/AEC), Sarabhai (PRL/ISRO), Bhatnagar (CSIR) created durable research bases |
| Science for development | Swaminathan (Green Revolution), Kurien (White Revolution), Kalam (defence/space) → food, milk, strategic self-reliance |
| Recognition & gaps | Nobels abroad (Khorana, Ramakrishnan) and under-recognition at home (Subbarao, Saha) raise the brain-drain and R&D-funding debate |
| AP angle | Subbarao (Bhimavaram), Raman's Visakhapatnam link, women leaders (Nigar Shaji, Aditya-L1) |
| Way forward | retain talent, raise R&D spend (~0.64% of GDP), strengthen ANRF-era institution-building |

**Data, provisions and examples to quote**
- **Science Nobels linked to India**: Raman (1930), Khorana (1968), Chandrasekhar (1983), Ramakrishnan (2009).
- **Bharat Ratna scientists**: Raman (1954), Kalam (1997), C.N.R. Rao (2014), Swaminathan (2024).
- **Institution milestones**: TIFR (1945), PRL (1947), ISRO (1969); SSB Prize for under-45 scientists.
- **Science-for-development**: Green Revolution (food self-sufficiency), Operation Flood (world's largest milk producer).
- **AP**: Yellapragada Subbarao (folic acid, methotrexate) of Bhimavaram as a point of state pride.

**Use in answers**
- Thesis line: "India's scientific rise rests as much on institution-building as on individual discovery."
- Pair each scientist with the institution or outcome they created (avoid a bare list of names).
- Link to the present: today's ANRF, missions and women mission-directors continue the same translation of research into capability.
- Diagram idea: an arrow chain — discovery → institution → policy → mass welfare.

**TL;DR**
- Serves Mains Paper-5 (M5-1): use scientists as evidence, not a list.
- Core argument: discovery + institutions + policy = nation-building; recognition gaps feed the brain-drain/R&D debate.
- Anchor sets: Nobels (1930/1968/1983/2009), Bharat Ratnas (1954/1997/2014/2024), institutions (TIFR/PRL/ISRO).
- AP angle: Subbarao of Bhimavaram and women mission-directors (Nigar Shaji, Aditya-L1).
keyPoints: Mains clause served: M5-1 (mains-5) — institutes in AP & India; prominent scientists.
Core argument: individual discovery becomes national strength only when institutionalised (Bhabha, Sarabhai, Bhatnagar).
Science-for-development anchors: Green Revolution (Swaminathan), White Revolution (Kurien), defence/space (Kalam).
Recognition sets: Nobels (1930/1968/1983/2009) and Bharat Ratnas (1954/1997/2014/2024); gaps feed the brain-drain debate.
AP angle: Yellapragada Subbarao of Bhimavaram and women mission-directors like Nigar Shaji (Aditya-L1).
